```{.r .cell-code}
clarkevans.test(childcareSG_ppp,
                correction="none",
                clipregion="sg_owin",
                alternative=c("clustered"))
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```

	Clark-Evans test
	No edge correction
	Z-test

data:  childcareSG_ppp
R = 0.53532, p-value < 2.2e-16
alternative hypothesis: clustered (R < 1)
```


:::
:::

The result here is clear, R is under 1, meaning the childcare centres are clustered rather than spread out randomly. Not surprising when you think about it, since childcare centres tend to open up near where families actually live, so they naturally bunch up around residential estates.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
clarkevans.test(childcareSG_ppp,
                correction="none",
                clipregion="sg_owin",
                alternative=c("clustered"),
                method="MonteCarlo",
                nsim=99)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```

	Clark-Evans test
	No edge correction
	Monte Carlo test based on 99 simulations of CSR with fixed n

data:  childcareSG_ppp
R = 0.53532, p-value = 0.01
alternative hypothesis: clustered (R < 1)
```


:::
:::

Same conclusion holds even with the Monte Carlo simulation approach - p value is still well under 0.05, so we can be confident this clustering isn't just random noise.


::: {.cell}

Now with all four planning areas tested, Choa Chu Kang and Tampines both show clustering, and it's worth checking whether Punggol and Jurong West follow the same pattern or not - planned towns like Punggol might actually be more evenly distributed since childcare centres get planned in from the start.

Went through G, F, K and L functions for Choa Chu Kang and Tampines — all four are basically different lenses on the same question (are these points clustered or not), and they consistently point the same direction. Good sanity check that the earlier Clark-Evans results weren't a fluke.
